```{r}
#| label: full_code_display

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1996)
beanie_prices <- tibble(
  listing_id = 1:300,
  price = round(rlnorm(n = 300, meanlog = log(15), sdlog = 0.8), 2)
)
labs_violin <- labs(
  title = "Beanie Babies resale prices",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "300 listings from 1998",
  x = "",
  y = "Price (USD)")
ggp2_violin <- ggplot(data = beanie_prices,
       aes(x = '', 
           y = price)) +
       geom_violin() 
ggp2_violin + 
  labs_violin
```

::::

## Description

Violin plots show data distribution and probability density. They are like box plots but have a rotated kernel density plot on each side. We can use them to compare data distribution across categories.

::: {.column-margin}

The violin plot is essentially a mirrored density plot, in which a smoothed distribution is plotted symmetrically across the `x` or `y` axis, creating a Rorschach-like inkblot area for the distribution:

![source: Rorschach test, Wikipedia](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/70/Rorschach_blot_01.jpg){fig-align="right" width="80%"}
:::

## Set up

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**PACKAGES:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
Install packages.
:::


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: pkg_code_violin
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DATA:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
In 1998, Beanie Babies were selling for wildly different prices: most went for a few dollars over retail, but a rare few sold for hundreds. We'll simulate 300 resale listings with `rlnorm()`, rounding each price to the nearest cent. Setting the seed with `set.seed()` means you'll get the same 300 prices every time you run the code below.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: data_code_violin
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
set.seed(1996)
beanie_prices <- tibble(
  listing_id = 1:300,
  price = round(rlnorm(n = 300, meanlog = log(15), sdlog = 0.8), 2)
)
glimpse(beanie_prices)
```
:::

## Distribution

Prices are a classic example of data that can't go below zero but can stretch a long way above it. That gives the violin a wide base and a long, thin neck. The trick to understanding this shape is the logarithm: on a log scale, these prices turn into the familiar bell curve from @sec-histograms. Below we'll move from the prices, to a picture, to the formula.

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**COUNT IT:**
:::

Start with the first ten listings.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_values_violin
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
head(beanie_prices$price, 10)
```
:::

Most of these sell for under \$30, but one listing is over \$100. A few expensive listings like this pull the mean well above the median. Taking the log of each price shrinks the gap.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_summary_violin
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
beanie_prices |> 
  summarise(
    mean = mean(price), 
    median = median(price),
    mean_log = mean(log(price)),
    median_log = median(log(price)))
```
:::

On the dollar scale, the mean is about \$`r round(mean(beanie_prices$price) - median(beanie_prices$price))` higher than the median. On the log scale, the mean and median are almost identical, which is what we'd expect from a symmetric distribution.

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DRAW IT:**
:::

A bar model splits the listings at \$15 (we'll see why in a moment). The two parts are close to equal, so \$15 sits near the middle of the prices.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: draw_bar_model_violin
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| fig-asp: 0.45
beanie_prices |> 
  mutate(range = factor(if_else(price < 15, "under $15", "$15 or more"),
    levels = c("under $15", "$15 or more"))) |> 
  count(range) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = "300 listings", fill = range)) + 
  geom_col(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) + 
  geom_text(aes(label = n), color = "white", 
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5, reverse = TRUE)) + 
  labs(x = "Number of listings", y = NULL, fill = "Price")
```
:::

Below are two violins of the same 300 prices. The first uses dollars, so most of the area is squashed near the bottom and the neck stretches up past \$100. The second puts the `y` axis on a log scale with `scale_y_log10()`, which turns the same prices into a symmetric shape centered near \$15.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: draw_violin
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| layout-ncol: 2
ggplot(data = beanie_prices, aes(x = "", y = price)) + 
  geom_violin() + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 15, linetype = "dashed") + 
  labs(title = "Dollar scale", x = NULL, y = "Price (USD)")

ggplot(data = beanie_prices, aes(x = "", y = price)) + 
  geom_violin() + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 15, linetype = "dashed") + 
  scale_y_log10() + 
  labs(title = "Log scale", x = NULL, y = "Price (USD, log scale)")
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**NAME IT:**
:::

The `rlnorm()` call that created the data draws from a [log normal distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-normal_distribution). A price is log normal when its logarithm is normal:

$$
\log(X) \sim \text{Normal}(\mu = \log(15), \sigma = 0.8)
$$

The two parameters describe the log scale, not the dollar scale. Back on the dollar scale, the median is $e^{\mu} = 15$ dollars, which is why the bar model split the listings at \$15. The mean is larger, $e^{\mu + \sigma^2 / 2} = 15 \times e^{0.32} \approx 20.66$ dollars, because the long right tail pulls it up. The bigger $\sigma$ gets, the longer the violin's neck and the further the mean drifts from the median.

Our simulated listings come close: the median is \$`r round(median(beanie_prices$price), 2)` and the mean is \$`r round(mean(beanie_prices$price), 2)`.


## Grammar 

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**CODE:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}

Create labels with `labs()`

Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data`

  - Place an empty string (`""`) in the `x` argument

Map an empty string (`""`) to the `x` and `price` to the `y`

Add `geom_violin()`

:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: code_graph_violin
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true 
#| warning: false
#| message: false
labs_violin <- labs(
  title = "Beanie Babies resale prices",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "300 listings from 1998",
  x = "",
  y = "Price (USD)")
ggp2_violin <- ggplot(data = beanie_prices,
       aes(x = '', 
           y = price)) +
       geom_violin() 
ggp2_violin + 
  labs_violin
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**GRAPH:**
:::

```{r}
#| label: create_graph_violin
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| layout-nrow: 1
labs_violin <- labs(
  title = "Beanie Babies resale prices",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "300 listings from 1998",
  x = "",
  y = "Price (USD)")
ggp2_violin <- ggplot(data = beanie_prices,
       aes(x = '', 
           y = price)) +
       geom_violin() 
ggp2_violin + 
  labs_violin
```
